title: Warm pools, Spot and the sweeper

story: Friday, 18:40. The orchestrator, the Temporal worker that claims VMs and drives every run, crashes in the middle of a CI-fixer run and comes back with a bug that keeps it from resuming that run. Its sandbox VM, a full-size machine, keeps running. Nothing is wrong with the VM itself; it is simply that nobody is using it anymore, and nobody remembers it is there. At about 42 cents an hour it would cost twenty dollars by Monday, and it is still a machine with our code on its disk.

In the same account, two VMs are stopped on purpose: one in the warm pool, waiting for the next run, and one that Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, parked while it waits for an answer on RH-1234. A cleanup job that only looks for "VMs nobody is using" could easily destroy one of those too.
hook.question: Who destroys a VM when whatever owned it is gone, without ever destroying one that is still in use?

read.h: Every VM has exactly one owner
p: A sandbox VM always belongs to exactly one of three owners, and its tags say which. While it waits in the warm pool, a group of stopped VMs that are already set up, the Auto Scaling group owns it; the tag aws:autoscaling:groupName says so. When a run claims it, the claim activity detaches it from the group and tags it with ai-agents:run-id, so from then on Temporal owns it, through the run's workflow. And when its owner is gone, it belongs to the sweeper, a small job that runs every 15 minutes and destroys whatever nobody owns.

The hard part is the middle owner, because a workflow cannot wave from inside the AWS console. So a run proves it is alive with a lease: the tag ai-agents:lease-until holds a time a little in the future, and the live run moves it forward every five minutes. A crashed orchestrator stops moving it. The sweeper never asks Temporal anything; it only reads tags, which is why it keeps working when Temporal itself is down.

The sweeper is a Python function on AWS Lambda, triggered every 15 minutes, with a role that can only terminate machines tagged ai-agents:managed=true. Each rule covers one owner that has gone away. A VM with a run-id whose lease has passed has lost its run, like the Friday VM. A VM stopped for more than 72 hours is retired, because its work is already saved at every checkpoint. A warm VM older than 24 hours is recycled inside its group, so the pool refills from the newest image. And a disk that belongs to no machine is deleted.
The lab runs these rules on a pretend fleet every 15 minutes of a pretend week, so you can watch each rule fire on the VM it was written for.

deeper.h: Go deeper: how the pool and Spot fit in
p: Each size has its own group with a warm pool of stopped VMs (two lite, two full and none wide to start, at most three at a time) and reuse on scale-in turned off, so a used VM never goes back. A new pool VM runs its slow setup once, starts and stops FCP Lab, and only then tells the group that setup is done, through a lifecycle hook; a stopped VM costs only its disk, about 8 to 10 dollars a month.

Routines that can simply retry, such as the CI fixer, use separate Spot groups, where AWS sells spare machines cheaply but can take one back with two minutes' notice. They have no warm pool. When the notice comes, the harness saves a checkpoint and exits as preempted, and the workflow retries on a fresh VM. Nova and the bug fixers stay on normal on-demand machines, because they wait on people.

The output above has a bug, and it is a bug of ownership. When Nova parks a VM while it waits for a person, the workflow stops it and sets its lease to 73 hours from now. The workflow still owns it: after 72 hours stopped, its own timer starts the VM, pushes a final checkpoint, and terminates it. But the sweeper's "stopped for over 72 hours" rule does not look at the lease. If the workflow's timer is a little late, here because the worker was restarting, the sweeper destroys the VM fifteen minutes before its owner arrives to save it.

The fix is to let the sweeper act only on VMs nobody owns. A VM with a fresh lease is owned, however long it has been stopped, so the stopped rule must also require that the lease has passed. The extra hour between 72 and 73 is the workflow's time to do its own cleanup, and the sweeper stays the job for leftovers only.

lab.title: A week of sweeping
lab.goal: Run the sweeper's rules over a pretend week, see each rule catch the VM it was written for, then find and fix the rule that destroys a VM its owner still needs.

guess.q: A claimed VM is running and its lease-until is 30 minutes in the past. Its run's workflow is still open in Temporal. What does the sweeper do on its next pass?

options.text: It terminates the VM, because the lease has passed.
options.why: The sweeper trusts only tags. A live run renews its lease every five minutes, so a lease that ran out means the run has stopped looking after its VM.

options.text: It asks Temporal whether the run is still open, and leaves the VM alone.
options.why: The sweeper never talks to Temporal, so it keeps working when Temporal is down. The lease is the only signal.

options.text: It stops the VM and keeps its disk, to be safe.
options.why: Stopping would leave an orphan that costs money. The sweeper's job is to remove what nobody owns.

lab.build: Add the fourth rule, for orphan disks. Give the simulation a list of volumes, each with an id, a status ("in-use" or "available") and tags, and make sweep() delete every available volume tagged managed (print "delete-volume vol-1 orphaned disk"). Add one available managed volume, one in-use managed volume and one available volume without the managed tag, and show that only the first one is deleted.
lab.fix: Now fix the real bug. The stopped-for-72-hours rule destroys the parked VM while its workflow still owns it, whenever the workflow's timer is a little late. Change only that rule so it also requires the lease to have passed, run python3 sweep.py with RETIRE_DELAY = 0.5, and check that the parked VM is retired by its workflow at hour 82.5 instead of by the sweeper.
checks: The crashed run's VM is terminated about two hours after its last lease renewal, and the live run's VM is never touched.
The warm VM is recycled just after 24 hours.
Before your fix, the parked VM is terminated at 82.25 h and its retire step fails.
After your fix, the parked VM is retired by the workflow at 82.5 h, and the sweeper prints nothing for it.
Your volume rule deletes only the available disk that carries the managed tag.

explain: Which three owners can a sandbox VM have, and which tag tells the sweeper which one it is?
Why does the sweeper read leases instead of asking Temporal whether a run is alive?

check.q: The orchestrator crashes and never resumes a run. What tells the sweeper that the run's VM is now nobody's?

options.text: Temporal marks the run as failed and the sweeper reads that
options.why: The sweeper never talks to Temporal, so it works even when Temporal is down.

options.text: The lease tag is no longer renewed, so its time passes
options.why: A live run moves ai-agents:lease-until forward every five minutes. A lease in the past means the owner is gone.
A VM waiting on a person is idle too, and is still owned. Only the lease says who owns it.

check.q: Nova parked a VM 72 hours and 10 minutes ago, and its lease runs until 73 hours after parking. The workflow's retire step has not run yet. With the corrected rules, what does the sweeper do?

options.text: Terminates it, because it has been stopped for over 72 hours
options.why: That was the bug: it destroys a VM whose owner is about to save it.

options.text: Starts it and pushes a checkpoint itself
options.why: Saving work is the workflow's job. The sweeper only removes what nobody owns.

options.text: Nothing, because the lease is still in the future, so the workflow still owns it
options.why: The lease is set one hour past the retire time exactly so the workflow can do its own cleanup first.

check.q: Why does the sweeper recycle warm-pool VMs older than 24 hours?

options.text: So the pool refills from the newest image instead of keeping old ones for days
options.why: A new image is built every night. Recycling makes the pool follow it within a day.

options.text: Because stopped VMs become more expensive after a day
options.why: A stopped VM costs the same for its disk every day. The reason is the image, not the price.

options.text: Because AWS deletes warm VMs after 24 hours anyway
options.why: AWS keeps them as long as the pool asks for them. The 24 hours are our rule.

p: modules/aws-sandbox-pool has one Auto Scaling group per size (desired 0, min 0, max 3) with a Stopped warm pool from var.warm_pool_size (lite 2, full 2, wide 0) and reuse_on_scale_in = false, an initial lifecycle hook on launch (heartbeat 1800 s, default ABANDON) completed by the sandbox-warm unit after FCP Lab started once, and Spot groups for lite and full (0% on-demand, price-capacity-optimized, m8i/m7i/m6i overrides, no warm pool). Claimed VMs are detached and owned by Temporal; the account's On-Demand and Spot vCPU quotas are the final cap.

modules/aws-sandbox-sweeper is a copy of modules/aws-vm-autostop: EventBridge rate(15 minutes), a Python Lambda outside the VPC, IAM limited to ai-agents:managed=true and the sandbox groups, dry_run on at first, one JSON line per action and the CloudWatch metrics AIAgents/Sweeper (OrphansTerminated, VolumesDeleted). Its stopped-over-72-hours rule should also require an expired lease, so it never races the workflow's retireSandbox (lease now + 73 h).

tickets.why: The warm pools per size, the setup-before-stop hook and the Spot groups.
The sweeper: its four rules, its tag-scoped role, dry run first and its metrics.
parkSandbox sets the 73-hour lease and retireSandbox checkpoints after 72 hours, the owner the sweeper must not race.

words.plain: Stopped VMs that are already set up, waiting so a run gets one in about a minute.
A tag with a time a little in the future; the live run keeps moving it, so a lease in the past means the owner is gone.
A Lambda that runs every 15 minutes and destroys sandbox VMs and disks that nobody owns.
Spare AWS machines sold cheaply, which AWS can take back with two minutes' notice.
Whoever is responsible for a VM right now: its Auto Scaling group, a live run, or, when both are gone, the sweeper.

review.q: Write the sweeper's four rules from memory, each with the owner it replaces.
review.a: Run-id with an expired lease: the run is gone. Stopped over 72 hours with an expired lease: retired work nobody came back for. Warm VM older than 24 hours: the pool, so it follows the newest image. Available managed disk: a machine that no longer exists.

review.q: A teammate wants the sweeper to ask Temporal which runs are open instead of reading leases. What do you answer?
review.a: The sweeper is the last line of cleanup and must work when Temporal or the orchestrator is down. Tags and leases need nothing but EC2, and a live run renews its lease every five minutes anyway.

remember: Every VM has one owner at a time, written in its tags: the pool, a live run with a fresh lease, or nobody, and only what nobody owns belongs to the sweeper.
